seoTitle: How to Create a Simple Form in Confluence Easily (2026)
metaDescription: Build a lightweight data-collection form in Confluence with a table, and know when to move up to a native Database or a paid marketplace form app instead.
intro: Confluence still doesn't ship with a dedicated drag-and-drop form builder, but you don't need one to collect structured input from a team. A table with clearly labeled columns does the job for most internal use cases, and it lives right inside the page your team already reads. This guide walks through building that kind of lightweight form from a blank page: setting up the field columns, publishing it, and recording an entry. It also covers where to look if a table starts to strain, since Confluence now offers a native alternative between a plain table and a paid form add-on.
prerequisites: Edit permission on the Confluence space where the form page will live
costNote: Building the form as a plain table, or as a native Database, costs nothing beyond your existing Confluence plan. Forms for Confluence and similar marketplace apps are paid add-ons, priced separately in the Atlassian Marketplace.

steps.heading: Start a new page for your form
steps.body: From your space's content tree, create a new page and give it a clear, purpose-built title. "Creating Form" is a fine working title while you build it out, though you'll want something more specific once it's live, like "Event RSVP" or "Bug Report Intake." The page starts blank except for the title and author byline, with the editor toolbar along the top offering formatting, tables, and other block types you'll insert next.

image.caption: A new draft page titled "Creating Form," with an empty table just inserted and the "/ to insert" prompt ready for the next block.

steps.heading: Insert a table and name your fields
steps.body: Type / to open the insert menu and choose a table, or use the table icon in the toolbar. This is the actual mechanism behind a Confluence "form" when you're not using a marketplace add-on: each column header becomes a field label, and each row underneath becomes one person's submission. Label the header row with exactly what you want to capture: Name, Email, Topics, Comments. Keep labels short enough that the columns stay readable once real answers are typed in.

image.caption: The table with its header row labeled Name, Email, Topics, and Comments: the field structure that stands in for a form in plain Confluence.

steps.heading: Test it with a sample entry
steps.body: Before sharing the page, fill in one row yourself to confirm the columns hold up under a real answer. Long email addresses, multi-word topics, and longer comments can force awkward text wrapping if a column is too narrow. Adjust column widths so the table stays scannable instead of cramped.

steps.heading: Publish the page
steps.body: Click Publish once the structure and a test row look right. Confluence confirms with a "Page successfully published" notice and offers a Share page link and a Copy link shortcut, so you can send the page straight to whoever needs to fill it in. The row you tested with, a sample entry from "Josh" with an email, topic, and short comment, stays on the page as a working example of what a completed entry looks like, which doubles as an implicit instruction for the next person filling it in.

image.caption: The published page with one filled-in row, plus the publish confirmation offering Share page and Copy link options.

steps.heading: Collect entries as new rows
steps.body: Once published, anyone with edit access can add a row underneath the existing ones by clicking into the last cell and pressing Tab, or by using the row-add control at the bottom of the table. Every submission stays visible on one page instead of scattered across separate documents, and because it's a normal Confluence table, you can sort, filter, or copy the data into a spreadsheet later without any export step.

steps.heading: Know when you need more than a table
steps.body: A table works well for a small internal group filling in a handful of rows, but it breaks down once you need validation on required fields, conditional questions that only appear based on a previous answer, or an automatic alert the moment someone submits. Confluence Cloud now also has a native Database object, a step up from a plain table with defined field types (text, number, date) and Table, Card, and Board views you can filter and sort. Try it before reaching for a paid tool, though it still won't validate an entry or notify you when one arrives. For that, a marketplace app such as Forms for Confluence adds a proper submission dashboard, field types like checkboxes and date pickers, and notification routing that neither a table nor a Database provides on its own.

troubleshooting.problem: Someone who needs to submit an entry can't add a row
troubleshooting.cause: Adding a row requires edit access to the page, not just view or comment access. Unlike a real form tool, a table-based form has no public-submission mode.
troubleshooting.fix: Grant edit access on the space or page to anyone who needs to submit, or move the form to a Database or marketplace app if wider, view-only submission is needed.

troubleshooting.problem: The table gets hard to scan once it has dozens of rows
troubleshooting.cause: A plain table has no built-in filtering, sorting, or alternate view.
troubleshooting.fix: Migrate the data into a Confluence Database, which supports Table, Card, and Board views plus filtering and sorting, or export it to a spreadsheet.

faq.question: Does Confluence have a native form builder?
faq.answer: Not a dedicated drag-and-drop one, as of September 2026. The built-in options are a plain table or, for more structure, a native Database object with defined field types and multiple views. Neither validates required fields, branches on conditional logic, or sends a notification on submission.

faq.question: How do people submit answers to a table-based form?
faq.answer: Anyone with edit access adds a new row underneath the existing ones, filling in each column the same way the sample row was filled in. There's no separate submission screen; the page itself is the form.

faq.question: Can I get notified when someone fills in the form?
faq.answer: Not automatically, whether you're using a plain table or a Database. For submission alerts, conditional questions, or a dedicated response dashboard, you'd need a marketplace form app.

faq.question: Can I turn the collected table data into a chart?
faq.answer: Not directly from a plain table. Copy the data into a Confluence Database, which supports Card and Board views, or export it to a spreadsheet for charting.

faq.question: What should I title a form page in Confluence?
faq.answer: Something specific to what you're collecting, such as "Event RSVP" or "Bug Report Intake" instead of a generic working title, so it's easy to find in the space tree and obvious what it's for once shared.
